title: Creational Patterns: Controlling How Objects Get Made
oneLiner: Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Singleton and Prototype, each with C#, a real .NET example and the interview angle.
keyTakeaway: Creational patterns move the `new` keyword out of the code that uses an object. Once the caller only asks for "something that is an IShape" or "a configured HttpClient", you can change which class gets built, or how, in one place. In modern .NET the DI container already does a lot of this, so reach for a hand written factory or singleton only when the container cannot express what you need.
explanation:
Every object has to be constructed somewhere. When that construction is a plain `new Circle()` in the middle of business logic, the business logic is now welded to the Circle class: it cannot be tested with a fake, and adding a new shape means editing it. Creational patterns are the standard ways of separating "I need one of these" from "here is exactly how one gets built".

The five here differ in what they hide. Factory Method hides which concrete class you get. Abstract Factory hides which whole family of related classes you get, so they always match. Builder hides a long, step by step construction behind readable calls. Singleton hides that there is only one instance. Prototype hides construction entirely by copying an existing object.

Pick a pattern. Each one shows the intent, when to use it and when not to, a small structure diagram, idiomatic C#, where you have already met it in .NET or in this app, and what interviewers actually probe for.
